paper_title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to single softmax. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Weight tying uses the same table for the input embedding and output layer of language model (Press & Wolf, 2017; Inan et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2024; Qwen Team, 2025). The table RV maps each input token to vector and, in its role as the unembedding, scores every vocabulary entry as possible next token. Sharing these roles saves matrix, substantial fraction of small models parameters. Tying also improved perplexity in the original experiments (Press & Wolf, 2017), and the fully untied 400M control in Batley & Saha (2026) underperformed its tied baseline. Both roles contribute to learning, but early in training the tied matrix is shaped mostly by output gradients (Lopardo et al., 2026). The usual tied head scores the vocabulary with single table followed by softmax. Its matrix of log-probabilities across contexts has rank at most + 1, limiting its ability to represent high-rank next-token distributions. This restriction is known as the softmax bottleneck (Yang et al., 2018). It matters when the next token has several plausible modes (Chang & McCallum, 2022) and has been linked to the saturation of small models (Godey et al., 2024). mixture of softmaxes (MoS) addresses the restriction by combining predictions from transformed contexts under one table, at cost of vocabulary projections per position (Yang et al., 2018). Two obvious fixes are to untie the output table or to add second softmax component under the tied table. Neither works well in our controls. An untied head adds parameters but gives up inputoutput sharing, and finishes 0.009 nats above the tied baseline at 142M. (b) Final 40-TPP loss of onóna minus Standard  (Table 1)  at 142M (top) and 330M (bottom); more negative is better. Dashed lines mark Standard. One seed per bar, so no error bars. We want instead head that gains capacity while every table used to score the vocabulary stays tied to the input. Twin embeddings with tied unembeddings implement this design with two tables of the same shape, and (Figure 1). The body reads their average = 1 2 (A + B), which serves as single input table. The head scores the vocabulary with both tables and mixes the resulting distributions using weight gt that depends only on the input token xt. We call this model onóna. Whereas MoS combines contexts under one table, onóna combines two tables under one context. It adds second table and gate weights, and each tied table receives its own output-projection gradient. Conditioning the gate on token identity allows its values to be computed once for the whole vocabulary, following the use of token identity in hash-based expert routing (Roller et al., 2021). At serving time, the input tables fold into and the gate becomes lookup in vector of values. The output still requires two vocabulary projections. We train Qwen3-style decoders on ClimbMix (Diao et al., 2025) at 142M, 330M and 1B. At 142M, onóna lowers final validation loss by 0.0285 nats for Dense, 0.0134 for the Gated DeltaNet hybrid, 0.0116 for MoE and 0.0226 for Attention Residuals. At 330M, the corresponding improvements are 0.0065, 0.0037, 0.0144 and 0.0119 nats. Both external perplexity benchmarks improve in all eight pairs, and all sixteen one-table ablations have higher loss than their mixture  (Table 1)  . The gains extend to the 1B Dense, GDN hybrid and AttnRes models. The 1B MoE model, however, has worse validation loss and perplexity despite higher downstream average  (Table 2)  . We make four contributions. 1. Twin tied tables for embedding and unembedding. We introduce onóna, which ties both vocabulary tables to the output head, feeds their average to the unchanged Transformer body, and mixes their two softmax distributions. 2. gate that reads only the input token. The mixture weight depends on the current token rather than the hidden state. At serving time, the input tables fold into their average and the gate becomes lookup of precomputed values. Exact scoring and greedy decoding still require two vocabulary projections (2 and Appendix B). 3. Evaluation across four architectures and three sizes. We train Dense, GDN hybrid, MoE and AttnRes models at 142M, 330M and 1B with equal token budgets within each size. Eleven of twelve pairs improve validation loss and both external perplexity benchmarks, and ten improve the eight-task accuracy average (Tables 12). 4. Controls and ablations. We compare against an untied head, MoS, input-only gating and deeper baseline. In 2 2 inputoutput ablation, neither role of the second table recovers the gain on its own (4). 2 class TwinTables(nn.Module): def __init__(self, V, d, std=0.02): super().__init__() self.A = nn.Parameter(std*torch.randn(V, d)) self.B = nn.Parameter(std*torch.randn(V, d)) self.w = nn.Linear(d, 1, bias=False) def merged(self): # M: the served input table return 0.5 * (self.A + self.B) def embed(self, ids): # train = serve return F.embedding(ids, self.merged()) def gate_logit(self, x0): # x0 = M[ids] # reads the input token only return self.w(F.rms_norm(x0, x0.shape[-1:])) # TwinTables, continued def log_probs(self, h, x0): # h: [B,T,d] = self.gate_logit(x0).float() la = (h @ self.A.T).float() lb = (h @ self.B.T).float() la = F.log_softmax(la, -1) lb = F.log_softmax(lb, -1) # log g, log(1-g): finite if saturates return torch.logaddexp( la + F.logsigmoid(z), lb + F.logsigmoid(-z)) # training step (body unchanged) x0 = twin.embed(ids) = final_norm(body(x0)) logp = twin.log_probs(h, x0) loss = F.nll_loss(logp.flatten(0, 1), tgt.flatten()) Figure 2: onóna pseudocode. The body reads averaged embeddings, and the head combines two tied softmax distributions using an input-token gate. Appendix provides implementation and serving details.

sections.title: 2 TWIN EMBEDDINGS WITH TIED UNEMBEDDINGS
sections.content: onóna expands the output family of tied language model by sharing two vocabulary tables between the input and output. Their average feeds single decoder, whose hidden state is projected through each table to form two softmax distributions. token-conditioned gate combines these distributions. We first describe the single-table model and its output restriction, then define the twin tables and gate before discussing their expressivity and cost. 2.1 PRELIMINARIES Given token sequence x1, . . . , xn over vocabulary of size , decoder-only language model (Vaswani et al., 2017) with tied embeddings (Press & Wolf, 2017; Inan et al., 2017) computes the next-token distribution in three stages. Embedding lookup. The token at position is mapped to row of the embedding table RV according to ej = Exj . (1) The decoder processes the embedding sequence to produce contextual hidden state ht at each position t. Unembedding (LM head). The output layer uses the same table to score the vocabulary and predict the next token, zt = Eht, Each row receives gradients from its input and output roles. p(xt+1 xt) = softmax(zt)xt+1. (2) Softmax bottleneck. The matrix of log-probabilities across contexts has rank at most + 1 (Yang et al., 2018). mixture of softmaxes (MoS) can exceed this bound by combining distributions from transformed hidden states under one shared table, p( xt) = (cid:88) k=1 πk(ht) softmax(cid:0)E tanh(Wkht)(cid:1), (3) where πk 0 and (cid:80) πk = 1. This requires vocabulary projections per position. 2.2 ARCHITECTURE OF ONÓNA onóna has three components. Twin embedding averages two input representations, twin unembedding produces two output distributions from the same hidden state, and token gate learns how to combine them (Figure 1(a)). The input and output components share the learned tables A, RV d. 3 Twin embedding. Each input representation is the arithmetic mean of the corresponding rows in the two tables, = 2 (A + B), ej = Mxj . (4) fixed average gives both tables symmetric input role without an input router, and it keeps the representation width, so the decoder is untouched. Twin unembedding. Each table scores the same ht. We normalize the two logit vectors separately and then combine their probabilities, p( xt) = gt softmax(Aht) + (1 gt) softmax(Bht). (5) The input average is fixed; only the output mixture weight is learned. Normalizing the two logit vectors separately is what lets the head go beyond single softmax. Mixing before the softmax, as in softmax(M ht), would keep the single-softmax restriction. Token gate and training. vector Rd maps the input tokens averaged embedding to the mixture weight, zt = rmsnorm(Mxt), gt = σ(zt). (6) Because the gate reads only the token, each token type learns one mixture weight, which can be precomputed for serving. The gate itself ignores context, but both component distributions depend on it through ht. Tables, gate and decoder are trained jointly on the next-token negative log-likelihood. Figure 2 gives log-space implementation, and Appendix covers the gradient paths and token routing. 2.3 PROPERTIES AND COMPUTATIONAL COST Tying and expressivity. Both scoring tables also serve as input tables. Mixing their distributions after the softmax can exceed the single-softmax + 1 rank bound; Appendix gives an explicit construction and contrasts it with mixing the tables before the softmax. The tied baseline is special case, since = = recovers it for every gate value. Our experiments do not start from this construction; the two tables are initialized independently (Appendix C). Relation to MoS. MoS combines distributions from transformed hidden states under one table, whereas onóna uses two tables with the same hidden state. The gate in onóna depends on token identity, while MoS uses contextual prior. Sections 3.3 and 4.1 compare the two designs empirically. Cost. The second table and gate vector add + trainable parameters, and training evaluates both output components, incurring extra projection FLOPs. At inference, conditional computation can avoid this extra projection, analogous to sparse activation in MoE (Fedus et al., 2022). The input tables fold into and gate values are precomputed. For untruncated sampling at temperature 1, we first select component with probability gt and then compute only its vocabulary projection and softmax. This produces an exact sample from the mixture, restricting the extra projection cost to training for this generation setting. Exact scoring, greedy decoding, and other temperatures or topk/top-p truncation generally still require both projections. Appendix gives the sampling argument, memory costs and measured throughput.

sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 3.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Models and data. We train Qwen3-style decoders (Qwen Team, 2025) from scratch on ClimbMix (Diao et al., 2025) at 142M, 330M and 1B scales, using GPT-2 BPE (Radford et al., 2019) and 1,024-token contexts. The four architectures are Dense, GDN hybrid (Yang et al., 2025), MoE (Fedus et al., 2022) and AttnRes (Kimi Team, 2026). At 142M and 330M, they share depth and width, with MoE active parameters matched to Dense. The smaller models use common 7.18B-token training pool, and the 1B models use disjoint 23.9B-token pool. Training repeats data when the token budget exceeds the pool size. 4 Training and comparisons. All experiments, including controls, use budget of 40 tokens per parameter (TPP) based on the Dense Standard parameter count. Variants at each size therefore receive the same number of training tokens. We use AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with warmup stabledecay schedule (Hu et al., 2024). Standard uses single tied table. onóna retains its decoder body and changes the vocabulary tables and output head. The twin tables are initialized independently, so their average has lower initial variance than the Standard input table. We compare alternative output layers in Section 3.3 and examine component and resource controls in Section 4. Appendix provides model configurations, hyperparameters and initialization details, and Appendix lists the implementation names.

sections.title: 4 ABLATION ANALYSIS
sections.content: The main results leave three questions open. Is the gain just extra vocabulary capacity, or just extra output computation (Section 4.1)? How much comes from the second tables input role, its output role, and their interaction (Section 4.2)? And would the same budget be better spent on decoder depth (Section 4.3)? Neither extra vocabulary capacity nor second softmax on its own reproduces the gain under this recipe. Section 3.3 covers further output layers in separate matched group. Input-side routing. learned input mixture with an averaged single-table head lowers loss by 0.009 nats at 142M, against 0.023 for onóna, both relative to the two-seed Standard mean. That is less than half the gain, but this control changes both the input rule and the head, so the remaining gap cannot be pinned on output gating alone. 4. INTERACTION BETWEEN INPUT AND OUTPUT ROLES Matched factorial design. To separate the input and output roles, we train 2 2 grid of 142M Dense models. The input is either or the fixed average (A + B)/2, and the output is either the softmax or the gated two-table mixture. Each cell is trained from scratch, so it adapts to its configuration, unlike the A-only/B-only ablations of trained checkpoint. All four cells share seed 0, initial body and weights, data order, optimizer schedule, token budget and 1,024 validation windows (Appendix B). The input-only cell uses fixed average, not the learned input gate of the control above. Joint contribution and interaction. Input averaging alone lowers loss by 0.00729 nats; the output mixture alone raises it by 0.00716  (Table 6)  . Together they lower it by 0.02002. All three two-table cells have the same 2V vocabulary parameters, and the mixture adds only d-parameter gate, so the extra vocabulary matrix by itself does not explain the joint models advantage over either single change. The output mixture helps with averaged inputs and hurts with single-table inputs. Writing Lij for the loss, with = 1 for twin embeddings and = 1 for twin unembeddings, the difference between the 8 two effects is = (L10 L11) (L00 L01) = 0.01990 nats. The interaction is positive: the joint reduction exceeds the sum of the two single-change effects, so in this grid the two roles are complementary. (7)

sections.title: 4.3 DEPTH AS AN ALTERNATIVE USE OF RESOURCES
sections.content: To ask whether the same budget would do more inside the decoder, we deepen the 330M Standard from 24 to 28 layers, which roughly matches the added parameters and training FLOPs of onóna (Appendix B). Loss falls from 2.6426 to 2.6258, 0.0071 below onóna at 2.6329  (Table 5)  . In this comparison, depth is the better use of the budget. We have not run the corresponding 1B control.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Tied embeddings. Sharing the input and output tables (Press & Wolf, 2017; Inan et al., 2017) is standard in small and mid-sized models (Liu et al., 2024; Qwen Team, 2025). Output gradients largely shape the shared matrix early in training (Lopardo et al., 2026). The fully untied 400M control of Batley & Saha (2026) underperforms its tied baseline, consistent with our untying controls. Over-tokenized Transformers (Huang et al., 2025) increase input vocabulary capacity through extra tables while retaining single output table. Twin embeddings instead use two tables over the same vocabulary and tie both to the output. The softmax bottleneck. Yang et al. (2018) established the rank bound for single-softmax head and proposed MoS to overcome it. Subsequent work reduced the cost of richer output layers with Mixtape (Yang et al., 2019) and changed the output activation without adding parameters with Sigsoftmax (Kanai et al., 2018). Studies of the bottleneck link its effects to multi-mode next-token distributions (Chang & McCallum, 2022) and the saturation of small models (Godey et al., 2024). MoS and onóna increase output expressiveness in different ways. MoS varies the context under one table, while onóna varies the table under one context and uses token-dependent prior. Our MoS controls compare the two directly (Tables 5 and 3). Token-conditioned routing. Hash layers (Roller et al., 2021) route tokens to experts by identity rather than by learned function of context. They are competitive with learned routing in the reported sparse-model experiments. onóna also uses token identity, but learns soft output-mixture weights rather than fixed hash assignments. Each previous-token type learns how much the two tables contribute to the next-token distribution. Multiple embeddings per token. Multi-sense embeddings (Neelakantan et al., 2014) and dynamic meta-embeddings (Kiela et al., 2018) keep several input vectors per word and use context to select or attend among them. GloVe combines its two tables by summation at serving time (Pennington et al., 2014), while multi-embedding recommenders retain several tables per feature during serving (Guo et al., 2024). Twin embeddings also retain two vectors per token. Their distinguishing feature is that both tables are tied to the head, where their output distributions are mixed.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: onóna shares two vocabulary tables between input and output, feeds their average to the decoder, and combines their softmax distributions with gate conditioned only on the input token. At 142M and 330M, it lowers validation loss and both external perplexities for all four architectures. The downstream average improves in six of eight pairs, with small declines for 142M GDN hybrid and MoE. At 1B, Dense, GDN hybrid and AttnRes improve, while MoE has worse loss despite higher downstream average. In the ablations, neither role of the second table recovers the gain on its own, and neither untying nor MoS reproduces it under the tested recipe. The gain costs an extra vocabulary projection, and at 330M deeper Standard model does better with similar budget. We have not run multi-seed experiments or resource-matched comparison at 1B; Appendix lists the remaining limitations.

Because log is already normalized, the log-softmax inside the cross-entropy is no-op. x0 is not detached, so gate gradients reach the input rows through RMSNorm. Serving. Because the gate depends only on the token, we precompute = σ(rmsnorm(M )w) [0, 1]V and fold the input tables into . Exact scoring and greedy decoding still compute both projections Aht and Bht and both log-softmaxes at each position. Sampling at temperature 1 without truncation is cheaper: draw Bernoulli(gxt), then sample from softmax(Aht) or softmax(Bht) accordingly. This is an exact sample from the mixture with one projection. Other temperatures and top-k or top-p truncation act on the mixture and need both projections. Gradient paths and baseline containment. Each table receives its own output-projection gradient plus half of the gradient through = (A + B)/2, which covers both the decoder input and the token gate, since the gate input is not detached. With = = E, both output distributions equal the tied baselines and the mixture no longer depends on the gate, so copying tied checkpoints table into both tables and keeping its decoder preserves its predictions. The reported experiments do not use this construction; they initialize the two tables independently (Appendix C). Token routing and the MoS comparison. The gate learns one mixture weight per previous-token type, using token identity as in hash-based routing (Roller et al., 2021) but with learned soft weights instead of fixed assignments. MoS (Yang et al., 2018) uses transformed hidden states under one tied table with context-dependent prior; onóna uses one hidden state, two tables and tokendependent prior. At = 2 the MoS transformation matrices add 2d2 parameters, against for the second table, plus the gate parameters in each design. The gradient paths also differ: MoS sends every components gradient into the one input table, whereas each table in onóna gets its own output-projection gradient. Training overhead. The second table adds 38.6M parameters at 142M, 51.5M at 330M and 103M at 1B. Training also materializes two fp32 log-probability vectors per position. MMLU uses up to five shots with the truncation described in Appendix B. The reported average weights all eight tasks equally, and task samples and order are shared across arms. Run-to-run variation. In the separate control experiments, two 142M Standard seeds finish 0.008 apart (2.8777 and 2.8693). At 330M, two Standard runs differing only in GPU layout finish 0.001 apart. These are the only repeats we have; they are not uncertainty estimates for the primary singleseed results. The tables mark with the runs that use different number of GPUs from their Standard counterpart, with the same global batch and window order.

sections.title: E LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Each arm has one seed, so we cannot estimate seed-to-seed variance, even though the primary loss comparisons share validation windows. The separate 142M controls and additional evaluations use unequal numbers of validation windows, and hardware, GPU layout and software versions vary across runs. None of the downstream averages has confidence interval or replicate seed. Equal token budgets do not match parameters or FLOPs, since onóna adds table and projection; the roughly resource-matched depth control exists at 330M only. Width and depth change together between 142M and 330M, and the larger budget repeats the shuffled data, so the runs do not separate width, training length and data repetition. At 1B, MoE has worse loss and perplexity but better downstream accuracy. The 1B runs use separate validation windows, and we have no explanation for the disagreement. The baseline and twin models also start from input tables of different scale, and no control isolates that difference. The one-table ablations change input and output together, so their loss penalties show neither output-only specialization nor the source of the gain over Standard. We have not tested larger vocabularies or longer contexts, and we have not looked at which token types the gate assigns to which table.
